title: Last House on the Block
status: Proposed concept · not market-validated · working title not cleared
pitch: Scavenge the neighbourhood. Every shortcut you make brings it closer to your home.
positioning: First-person zombie survival with Project Zomboid’s ordinary-person vulnerability: familiar homes, scarce supplies, wounds that matter and a safehouse worth returning to. Firearms are a noisy last resort, not the main attraction.
differentiation: The testable angle is concentrated, visible cause and consequence: the route that makes a supply run easier also gives infected a way home. Noise, persistence and building are established mechanics—not inventions. The question is whether a short neighbourhood loop makes those trade-offs unusually readable and compelling.
demandLimit: These are selected comparables, not a market census. Their audiences demonstrate interest in survival games, not an unfilled gap, low acquisition cost or demand for this unbuilt concept. No paid-sales or organic-attribution claim is made.

comparables.title: Project Zomboid
comparables.observation: Looting, barricading, wounds and dangerous encounters support an ordinary survivor fantasy. It is not a first-person game.
comparables.metricCaveat: A 2026 peak for an established 2013 game—not evidence about a new launch’s odds.
comparables.borrow: Vulnerability and domestic detail—not its enormous accumulated simulation scope.
comparables.difference: A first-person view and a compact, legible route dilemma; neither is evidence of a market gap.

comparables.title: VEIN
comparables.status: First person · Early Access since 24 October 2025
comparables.observation: Already combines looting, crafting, base building, multiplayer and simulated power/water. Its Early Access notes separate playable systems from planned NPCs and settlements.
comparables.metricCaveat: A launch-era concurrency signal, not paid copies, profitability or proof of unpaid reach.
comparables.borrow: An immediate, grounded survival perspective—not a promise to match its sandbox breadth.
comparables.difference: Prove a short, authored shortcut-versus-safehouse loop. “Zomboid, but FPS” is already occupied.

comparables.title: 7 Days to Die
comparables.observation: Combines first-person combat, resource gathering, crafting, building and zombie survival.
comparables.metricCaveat: A historical 2024 full-release-period peak, not a 2026 new-release result.
comparables.borrow: A reason to scavenge now and prepare for danger later—not a vast destructible world.
comparables.difference: Ordinary-person scarcity and route consequences in a small neighbourhood, instead of escalating combat and construction scale.

demo: One small street, one safehouse and one scavenging interior. Two supply runs and one night, roughly 10–15 minutes. Single-player first; a second looting building is stretch scope.
fullGameDirection: If the loop earns repeat play, the full-game direction is a continuous, walkable neighbourhood: depleting houses, persistent access routes and a refuge improved with scavenged materials. Add adjacent streets and deeper survival choices only after validating the small loop. That larger open-world game is outside this sprint.
capacity: 15 working days × 2 senior developers + 1 artist = 45 maker-days. The PM and marketing manager add 30 person-days for scope, testing, research and communication—not extra programming capacity. This is a planning estimate, not a delivery guarantee.
loop: Leave home for food, scrap or cloth for bandages.
Choose a slower safe route or create a convenient shortcut.
Bring supplies back; craft a barricade repair or a bandage.
Survive the night through the routes you left open. Reconsider the next trip.

tradeoffs.consequence: Infected can cross the same opening
tradeoffs.implementation: One persistent flag switches a navigation connection; no destructible fence simulation.

tradeoffs.consequence: An authored motion-sensor event opens it noisily at night
tradeoffs.implementation: One powered flag, a trigger and a door animation; no electricity network.

tradeoffs.benefit: An easy escape on the return trip
tradeoffs.consequence: The opening leaves a direct approach to your barricade
tradeoffs.implementation: A fixed doorway and navigation link; no physics-based door AI.

scope: Four inventory slots and three useful resource families: food restores stamina, scrap repairs a barricade, cloth crafts a bandage. Two recipes and one barricade socket; no physical inventory simulation.
One enemy archetype, at most six active infected and fixed navigation with switchable links. A simple noise event changes the investigation target.
One melee tool; one pistol with scarce ammunition only if basic combat is stable. Gun noise raises a simple threat state. Cut the pistol before cutting the route-consequence loop.
One wound consequence: a lost carrying slot until treated. No nutrition, infection or detailed medical simulation.
Persist only explicit door, fence, power, loot, inventory and wound state across the two trips and night. A minimal local save is stretch scope; no simulated off-screen world.
cuts: No multiplayer, procedural map, vehicles, NPC survivors, weather, climbing, freeform construction, structural destruction, crafting tree or large weapon catalogue. Do not advertise the prototype as a complete open world.
pros: One reusable domestic environment puts limited art time into recognisable, lived-in spaces.
A visible shortcut → consequence chain can communicate the hook without explaining a large simulation.
The same street supports different route choices, allowing replay tests before adding more content.
cons: VEIN is a direct substitute. Perspective, zombies and crafting alone are not enough to distinguish this game.
First-person animation, hit feedback and enemy navigation can consume the entire sprint.
The shortcut dilemma could feel scripted, unfair or trivial. It needs clear warning cues and a meaningful alternative route.
A tiny solo demo will not satisfy the breadth or co-op expectations set by mature survival sandboxes.

weeks.label: Days 1–5
weeks.title: Prove the consequence
weeks.work: Developer A owns movement, interaction and inventory. Developer B owns enemy navigation and route flags. The artist builds one modular interior and street kit. PM runs scope and daily playtests. By day 4, a rough trip → consequence → night loop must work.

weeks.label: Days 6–10
weeks.title: Make the choice readable
weeks.work: Add the second run, two recipes, wound cost and the powered-garage event. Use light, sound and sightlines to foreshadow danger. Marketing recruits appropriate survival players; PM records unprompted explanations. Finish content by day 10.

weeks.label: Days 11–15
weeks.title: Stabilise and show it
weeks.work: Fix navigation, interaction failures and feedback. Record genuine prototype footage: a short consequence clip and an unedited full loop. Ship a labelled prototype/demo only if stable and Steam timing permits; otherwise deliver the playable build and honest video.

gates: Day 4: a complete rough loop works. If not, cut the garage event and pistol; keep one route choice with a clear consequence.
Day 7: changing the route visibly changes the night approach. If both choices play alike, revise the mechanic before producing more art.
Day 10: a proposed directional test is 4 of 5 unfamiliar testers explaining their own choice’s consequence without prompting. This tiny sample is a usability gate, not market validation.

Before expansion: compare hook comprehension, demo completion and voluntary replay between the shortcut version and a basic scavenging version. Set the success criteria before testing; no universal wishlist or view benchmark is assumed.
clip: Proposed 15-second prototype clip: 0–4s, carry supplies through the garage shortcut you proudly opened; 4–9s, show the motion sensor and noisy door activating at night; 9–15s, infected take that same route while you scramble to close your neglected barricade. The joke is your recognisable mistake—not a scripted marketing scene presented as gameplay.
marketing: Start with a few small creators who already cover grounded survival. Offer an unedited 10–15-minute build and ask whether the choice produces a story they want to tell. Compare the cause-and-consequence clip with ordinary scavenging footage. Label recruitment source, impressions, clicks and demo behaviour separately; views are not sales and public activity cannot establish organic attribution.
brief: Last House on the Block — first-person, solo zombie survival. Hypothesis: survival players value a readable dilemma where shortcuts for scavenging become infected routes to their safehouse. Compare Project Zomboid (vulnerability), VEIN (direct first-person substitute) and 7 Days to Die (scavenge/defend rhythm). Demo: one street, safehouse + one interior, two trips + one night, 10–15 minutes; 15 workdays / 45 maker-days. Test whether unfamiliar players can explain their own route choice’s consequence and choose to replay. Not proven: unmet demand, organic reach or sales. Scope risk: first-person feel and navigation; cut multiplayer, procedural worlds and freeform building. Evidence: https://store.steampowered.com/app/108600/ https://store.steampowered.com/app/1857950/ https://store.steampowered.com/app/251570/
